lines.text: A kingdom that vanished from the map and came back, again and again. This is the story of Poland, from its baptism to the European Union.
On the Vistula stood Krakow, the old royal capital where Poland's kings would be crowned.
In 966 Duke Mieszko the first was baptised, and with that act the Polish state is said to begin.
So began Poland, a country of central Europe whose borders and freedom would be won, lost and won again over a thousand years.
In April 1241 a Mongol army crushed Duke Henry of Silesia at Legnica. Henry fell, but the Mongols moved on and Poland rebuilt.
In 1410, at Grunwald, Poland and Lithuania together crushed the Teutonic Knights, one of the great battles of medieval Europe.
Nicolaus Copernicus dared to say the Earth travels around the Sun. His book came out the year he died, and the old picture of the heavens began to fall.
In 1569 Poland and Lithuania joined in a Commonwealth, with an elected king and a parliament of nobles, for a time among Europe's largest states.
In 1683 King John Sobieski led the army that broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, and the Ottoman retreat from central Europe began.
But a century later Russia, Prussia and Austria carved the Commonwealth up in three bites, and Poland disappeared from the map.
Between the partitions, in 1791, Poland adopted Europe's first modern written constitution, a last bold effort at reform.
Frederic Chopin left for Paris, and carried Polish dances into the piano music of the world.
In November 1830 Poles rose against Russian rule. The rising was crushed within a year, but the hope did not die.
Maria Sklodowska left Warsaw for Paris and became Marie Curie, discoverer of radium and of polonium, which she named for her homeland.
In 1918, as the First World War ended, Poland was reborn after more than a century.
Almost at once it fought the Soviets, and in 1920 turned them back at the Battle of Warsaw.
Karol Wojtyla would become Pope John Paul the second, and his support would give heart to those who challenged communist rule.
Wislawa Szymborska wrote short, witty poems about everyday things, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1996.
In September 1939 Germany invaded from the west and the Soviet Union from the east. The Second World War in Europe had begun.
In 1940, in the forest of Katyn and elsewhere, the Soviet secret police shot about twenty-two thousand Polish officers and leaders.
In occupied Poland the Nazis built Auschwitz, where more than a million people, most of them Jews, were murdered.
In Warsaw hundreds of thousands of Jews were sealed into a ghetto, where many died of hunger and disease.
From there most were sent to Treblinka, where some eight hundred thousand people were killed in little over a year.
In the spring of 1943 the Jews left in the ghetto took up arms. They were crushed, but their revolt became a lasting symbol of resistance.
In that same year a future leader was born. Lech Walesa, an electrician, would lead the strikes at the Gdansk shipyard.
In 1944 the Home Army rose against the Nazis in Warsaw. When it failed, the city was razed to the ground.
Donald Tusk, born in Gdansk, would serve twice as prime minister and lead the European Council.
Olga Tokarczuk, author of Flights and The Books of Jacob, would bring Poland another Nobel Prize in Literature.
In 1980 Solidarity was born at the Gdansk shipyard, the first free trade union in the Soviet bloc. Martial law banned it, but it came back.
Robert Lewandowski would grow up to captain Poland, one of the great goalscorers of his time.
In 1989 communists and Solidarity sat down at a round table, and agreed the first partly free elections in the Eastern Bloc.
In 2004 Poland joined the European Union together with nine other countries, a return to the heart of Europe.
Then in 2010 a plane crashed near Smolensk, killing the president and ninety-five others, and the whole nation mourned.
Erased, occupied and reborn, Poland has outlasted every attempt to remove it from the map.
